questions.q: Which part of a plant is the main food-making organ?
questions.explanation: Leaves contain chlorophyll and are where most photosynthesis takes place.

questions.q: Which source of energy is needed for photosynthesis?
questions.explanation: Sunlight provides the energy that chlorophyll uses to make food.

questions.q: Which of these is an insectivorous plant?
questions.explanation: The Venus flytrap traps insects and digests them.

questions.q: A leaf has green and white patches. After testing with iodine, only the green patches turn blue-black. What does this show?
options: Chlorophyll is needed to make starch
Iodine is absorbed only by green colour
Starch is made in the dark
questions.explanation: Only the green parts, which have chlorophyll, carried out photosynthesis and made starch.

questions.q: Which one of these is a heterotroph?
questions.explanation: A mushroom has no chlorophyll and depends on other organisms for food.

questions.q: Write the word equation for photosynthesis.
questions.answer: Carbon dioxide + water, in the presence of sunlight and chlorophyll, gives glucose (food) + oxygen.
keyPoints: Carbon dioxide and water are the raw materials
Glucose and oxygen are the products
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis changes carbon dioxide and water into glucose and releases oxygen.

questions.q: A strip of black paper is clipped over part of a leaf on a plant kept in sunlight for a few days. When the leaf is tested with iodine, the covered part does not turn blue-black. What is the conclusion?
options: Chlorophyll is absent in the covered part
Light is needed for the formation of starch
Water cannot reach the covered part
Carbon dioxide is made in the covered part
questions.explanation: The only difference between the two parts is light, so light is needed for starch formation.

questions.q: How does a parasitic plant differ from a saprotroph in the way it gets food? Give an example of each.
questions.answer: A parasite takes food from the body of a living host plant; Cuscuta is an example. A saprotroph takes food from dead and decaying matter; a mushroom is an example.
keyPoints: Parasite feeds on a living host
Saprotroph feeds on dead or decaying matter
questions.explanation: Both depend on others for food, but one uses living and the other dead organisms.

questions.q: Saliva in the mouth acts on which nutrient in food?
questions.explanation: Saliva turns starch into sugar.

questions.q: Where is the bile juice made by the liver stored until it is needed?
questions.explanation: The gall bladder stores bile.

questions.q: How many milk teeth do children usually have?
questions.explanation: A child has 20 milk teeth, which are later replaced by permanent teeth.

questions.q: In which organ is food churned with digestive juices to form a semi-liquid mixture?
questions.explanation: The muscular walls of the stomach churn food while it mixes with the gastric juices.

questions.q: The pancreatic juice acts on which nutrients?
questions.explanation: The pancreas makes a juice that digests carbohydrates, proteins and fats.

questions.q: What is the role of bile juice in digestion?
questions.answer: Bile breaks fats into very tiny droplets, which makes it easier for the enzymes to digest them. It is made by the liver and poured into the small intestine.
keyPoints: Made by the liver and released into the small intestine
questions.explanation: Bile helps digest fats.

questions.q: Grass-eating animals such as cattle have a longer small intestine than meat-eating animals such as lions. What is the best reason?
options: Plant food is bulky and harder to digest, so it takes longer to digest and absorb
questions.explanation: Cellulose-rich plant food needs more time and a longer path for digestion.

questions.q: Describe the path taken by a piece of bread from the mouth until the undigested part leaves the body.
questions.answer: Bread goes from the mouth down the food pipe to the stomach, then to the small intestine, then to the large intestine, and the undigested waste leaves through the anus.
questions.explanation: These organs together make up the alimentary canal.

questions.q: The pointed teeth in the human mouth used for tearing food are called:
questions.explanation: Canines are pointed and tear food.

questions.q: Wool is obtained from which part of a sheep?
questions.explanation: Wool is the hair (fleece) of a sheep.

questions.q: What is a cocoon?
questions.answer: A cocoon is the protective covering of silk thread that the silkworm spins around itself before it becomes a moth.
keyPoints: Spun by the silkworm before it turns into a moth
questions.explanation: Silk fibre is obtained from cocoons.

questions.q: Which of these fibres comes from an animal?
questions.explanation: Silk is an animal fibre, while cotton and jute are plant fibres.

questions.q: What do we call the process of taking out silk threads from cocoons?
questions.explanation: In reeling, silk threads are unwound from the cocoons.

questions.q: Wool and silk are both fibres made mostly of:
questions.explanation: Both wool and silk are protein fibres.

questions.q: Name any three steps in the processing of fleece into wool in the correct order, after shearing.
questions.answer: After shearing, the fleece is scoured (washed), then sorted by quality, then the burrs are picked out. Later the fibres are dyed and spun into yarn.
questions.explanation: Raw fleece is cleaned and sorted before it can be spun.

questions.q: Shearing does not hurt the sheep. What is the best reason?
options: Sheep have no feeling in their skin
Only the outer hair is cut, like a haircut, and the skin is not harmed
The sheep is made to sleep
questions.explanation: Shearing removes the hair and not the skin, and the hair grows back.

questions.q: Compare the sources of wool and silk.
questions.answer: Wool comes from the fleece or hair of animals such as sheep, goat and yak. Silk comes from the cocoon spun by the silkworm, which is the larva of the silk moth.
keyPoints: Wool from hair of animals like sheep, goat, yak
Silk from the cocoon of the silkworm
questions.explanation: Both are animal fibres but they come from different parts and animals.

questions.q: By which mode does heat mainly travel in liquids and gases?
questions.explanation: Liquids and gases transfer heat by the movement of the heated material, which is convection.

questions.q: Which one of these is a good conductor of heat?
questions.explanation: Metals like copper are good conductors.

questions.q: What is the range of a laboratory thermometer?
questions.explanation: A laboratory thermometer typically measures from -10 degrees C to 110 degrees C.

questions.q: While measuring the temperature of hot water with a laboratory thermometer, how should the bulb be placed?
options: Touching the bottom of the beaker
Touching the side of the beaker
Fully in the water without touching the bottom or sides
questions.explanation: Touching the bottom or sides would give the temperature of the glass, which may be hotter than the water.

questions.q: What is conduction of heat? Give an example.
questions.answer: Conduction is the transfer of heat through a substance from the hot part to the cooler part without the substance itself moving. For example, the handle of a metal spoon becomes hot when the other end is in hot tea.
keyPoints: Heat passes from particle to particle
questions.explanation: Conduction mainly takes place in solids.

questions.q: Why are dark-coloured clothes preferred in winter, if one wants to stay warm in the sunshine?
options: Dark colours absorb more heat from the Sun
questions.explanation: Dark surfaces absorb more heat radiation than light surfaces.

questions.q: Why do cooking vessels often have a copper or aluminium base?
questions.answer: Copper and aluminium are good conductors of heat. They quickly pass the heat from the flame to the food inside, so cooking is faster.
keyPoints: Copper and aluminium are good conductors
Heat passes quickly to the food
questions.explanation: Good conductors transfer heat rapidly from the flame to the contents.

questions.q: Which of these substances is basic in nature?
questions.explanation: Baking soda solution is basic and turns red litmus blue.

questions.q: Which acid is found in tamarind?
questions.explanation: Tamarind contains tartaric acid.

questions.q: Which natural indicator changes from yellow to red in a basic solution?
questions.explanation: Turmeric turns red with bases such as soap solution.

questions.q: Which acid is present in curd and sour milk?
questions.explanation: Lactic acid is formed in milk when it sours or turns to curd.

questions.q: What taste and feel are generally typical of bases?
options: Bitter and soapy to the touch
questions.explanation: Bases taste bitter and feel soapy, though one should never taste unknown chemicals.

questions.q: What is neutralisation? Give an example.
questions.answer: Neutralisation is the reaction between an acid and a base in which both lose their properties and form a salt and water. For example, hydrochloric acid with sodium hydroxide gives sodium chloride and water.
questions.explanation: Neutralisation cancels the acidic and basic nature of the two substances.

questions.q: A curry stain on a white shirt turns red when rubbed with soap but fades back to yellowish when the shirt is rinsed well with water. Why?
options: Water is an acid that makes the stain disappear
Turmeric changes colour in soap, and rinsing removes the soap, so the yellow returns
questions.explanation: Soap, a base, turns turmeric red; when the soap is washed out, the red colour is gone.

questions.q: You have three unlabelled colourless solutions: an acid, a base and a neutral solution. How can red and blue litmus papers be used to tell them apart?
questions.answer: Dip both a red and a blue litmus paper in each solution. The one that turns blue litmus red is the acid. The one that turns red litmus blue is the base. The one that changes neither is neutral.
questions.explanation: Litmus shows both acidic and basic nature.

questions.q: Tearing a sheet of paper into small pieces is which kind of change?
questions.explanation: The pieces are still paper, so no new substance is formed.

questions.q: What is the reddish-brown coating that forms on iron objects left in moist air called?
questions.explanation: Rust is the reddish-brown substance formed when iron reacts with oxygen and water.

questions.q: Stainless steel does not rust easily because it is:
options: Made of iron mixed with carbon and metals like chromium and nickel
questions.explanation: The alloy of iron with chromium, nickel and carbon resists rusting.

questions.q: Which products are formed when a candle burns completely in air?
questions.explanation: Wax contains carbon and hydrogen, which combine with oxygen to give carbon dioxide and water vapour.

questions.q: Name two things that may be observed during a chemical change.
questions.answer: Examples of what can be observed are a change in colour, release of a gas, production of heat or light, formation of a solid (a precipitate), or a change in smell.
keyPoints: Two correct observations such as colour change, gas, heat, light, precipitate
questions.explanation: These signs tell us that a new substance may be forming.

questions.q: Which one of these is NOT a sure sign of a chemical change?
options: Release of a gas with a new smell
Change in shape of a substance
Change in colour along with release of heat
questions.explanation: A change of shape alone, such as beating a metal into a sheet, can occur in a physical change.

questions.q: A cut apple turns brown if it is kept in the open for some time. Is this a physical or chemical change? Explain.
questions.answer: It is a chemical change. The cut surface reacts with oxygen of the air and a new brown substance forms, which cannot be changed back to the original.
keyPoints: Reaction with oxygen forms a new substance
questions.explanation: A new substance with a different colour forms, so the change is chemical.

questions.q: Which of the following is a chemical change that takes place in green leaves in sunlight?
questions.explanation: In photosynthesis, carbon dioxide and water change into glucose and oxygen, which are new substances.

questions.q: Which bird with a large colourful beak is found in tropical rainforests?
questions.explanation: The hornbill has a large beak and lives in tropical forests.

questions.q: Regions lying close to the equator are called:
questions.explanation: The tropical region lies close to the equator and is warm.

questions.q: The red-eyed tree frog of the rainforest has sticky pads on its feet. What does this help it to do?
options: Climb and cling to leaves and branches
questions.explanation: Sticky pads help the frog hold onto wet leaves and branches.

questions.q: Which of these describes polar regions?
options: Very cold and covered with ice and snow
questions.explanation: The polar regions near the North and South Poles are icy and very cold.

questions.q: Write two features that help animals live in the very cold polar regions.
questions.answer: Polar animals have a thick layer of fat under the skin and thick fur or feathers that keep heat in. Some, like the polar bear, are white, which helps them blend in with the snow.
keyPoints: Thick fat layer or fur to keep warm
White colour or another correct feature
questions.explanation: These features reduce heat loss and help with hunting in snow.

questions.q: Which feature helps a penguin move quickly in water?
questions.explanation: Penguins have a streamlined body and flippers that act like paddles.

questions.q: A forecast says, 'Tomorrow there will be 10 mm of rain in our city.' This statement is about:
questions.explanation: A forecast for one day describes weather, not the long-term average.

questions.q: Why are tropical rainforests home to a very large number of kinds of animals?
questions.answer: The warm and wet climate allows plants to grow all year, so there is plenty of food and shelter. Many different animals can find what they need.
keyPoints: Warm and wet climate throughout the year
questions.explanation: Abundant plant growth supports many kinds of animals.

questions.q: What is the sound heard after a flash of lightning called?
questions.explanation: Thunder is the sound produced by lightning.

questions.q: What is a cyclone over the north-western Pacific Ocean usually called?
questions.explanation: Tropical cyclones in the north-west Pacific are called typhoons.

questions.q: Which of these is a sensible preparation when a cyclone warning has been given?
options: Go to the beach to watch
Store drinking water, dry food and a torch
questions.explanation: People should be ready with essentials and move to safe places.

questions.q: Windmills use the energy of wind to generate electricity. Wind is described as:
options: A source that is used up quickly
questions.explanation: Wind keeps blowing, so it is a renewable source of energy.

questions.q: Give two uses of wind.
questions.answer: Wind turns windmills to generate electricity or to lift water. It also moves sailing boats, dries clothes and disperses seeds and pollen.
questions.explanation: Wind energy has been used by people for a very long time.

questions.q: Why does a hot-air balloon rise?
options: The hot air inside is lighter than the cooler air outside
The hot air inside is heavier than the air outside
The balloon is filled with water
questions.explanation: Heated air expands and becomes less dense, so the balloon floats up.

questions.q: During a thunderstorm we see lightning first and hear thunder a little later. Why?
questions.answer: Lightning and thunder happen at the same moment, but light travels much faster than sound. The light reaches our eyes almost at once, while the sound takes longer to arrive.
keyPoints: Light travels much faster than sound
questions.explanation: The delay between flash and thunder depends on how far away the lightning is.

questions.q: Which organs are the main organs of breathing in humans?
questions.explanation: Humans breathe with the help of the lungs.

questions.q: Which gas is given out as a waste product of respiration?
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide is produced and breathed out.

questions.q: What is the function of hair and mucus in the nose?
options: To trap dust and germs in the air we breathe in
questions.explanation: Hair and mucus filter the incoming air.

questions.q: A whale is a sea animal but it breathes with:
options: Lungs, coming to the surface to breathe
questions.explanation: Whales are mammals and have lungs, so they surface to breathe.

questions.q: Write the word equation for aerobic respiration.
questions.answer: Glucose + oxygen gives carbon dioxide + water + energy.
keyPoints: Carbon dioxide, water and energy are released
questions.explanation: In aerobic respiration, oxygen is used to break down glucose completely.

questions.q: Yeast is added to a sugar solution and kept warm. Which products form as it respires without oxygen?
questions.explanation: Yeast breaks down sugar to give alcohol and carbon dioxide, a process used in making bread and wine.

questions.q: Why do people who climb to a high mountain often breathe faster?
questions.answer: The air at high altitudes is thin and has less oxygen in each breath. The body breathes faster to try to get enough oxygen.
keyPoints: Less oxygen available at high altitude
Faster breathing takes in more air
questions.explanation: Breathing rate rises to make up for the lower oxygen content of each breath.

questions.q: What can we feel by placing fingers on the wrist?
questions.explanation: The pulse is the throbbing of an artery caused by the heartbeat.

questions.q: A person with anaemia has a shortage of:
questions.explanation: In anaemia there is not enough haemoglobin, so less oxygen is carried.

questions.q: Which instrument is used by a doctor to listen to the heartbeat?
questions.explanation: A stethoscope carries the sound of the heartbeat to the doctor's ears.

questions.q: Which tissue of the plant carries food from the leaves to other parts?
questions.explanation: Phloem carries the prepared food from the leaves.

questions.q: Besides plasma, name the three kinds of components in blood.
questions.answer: Red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets.
questions.explanation: Plasma carries these cells around the body.

questions.q: Which of these is a waste product removed by plants?
questions.explanation: Plants store waste in forms such as gums, resins and latex, and also lose it by shedding leaves.

questions.q: Why does blood in the veins not flow backwards?
options: Veins have valves that allow flow in one direction
questions.explanation: Valves in veins close to stop blood from flowing backwards.

questions.q: What would happen to a plant if all the xylem vessels in its stem were blocked?
questions.answer: Water and minerals could not reach the leaves. The leaves could not make food by photosynthesis, so the plant would wilt and eventually die.
keyPoints: No photosynthesis, so the plant wilts and dies
questions.explanation: Xylem is the only way water reaches the leaves.

questions.q: What is the process called by which a seed grows into a new plant (seedling)?
questions.explanation: Germination is the sprouting of a seed into a young plant.

questions.q: In which part of the stamen are the pollen grains made?
questions.explanation: Pollen is produced in the anther.

questions.q: Pollen falls on the stigma of a flower of another plant of the same kind. This is called:
questions.explanation: Transfer of pollen between flowers of different plants is cross-pollination.

questions.q: Winged seeds, such as those of the maple, are dispersed mainly by:
questions.explanation: The wings let the seeds drift in the wind.

questions.q: What is fragmentation? Name one plant that reproduces by it.
questions.answer: Fragmentation is a type of asexual reproduction in which the body of an organism breaks into pieces, and each piece grows into a new organism. Spirogyra, an alga, reproduces this way.
keyPoints: Body breaks into pieces that grow into new individuals
questions.explanation: Fragmentation is common in simple green algae like Spirogyra.

questions.q: Which part of a potato grows into a new plant?
questions.explanation: Each eye of a potato is a bud that can sprout a new plant.

questions.q: A flower has stamens but no pistil. Such a flower is called:
questions.explanation: A flower with only the male part is a unisexual male flower.

questions.q: Put these events in the correct order: seed formation, pollination, fertilisation.
questions.answer: Pollination first, then fertilisation, and finally seed formation.
questions.explanation: Seeds develop from fertilised ovules.

questions.q: Which instrument measures the distance travelled by a vehicle?
questions.explanation: The odometer records the distance covered.

questions.q: What is the SI unit of speed?
questions.explanation: Speed is distance divided by time, so its SI unit is metre per second.

questions.q: An old device that uses the shadow of a stick to tell the time of day is called a:
questions.explanation: A sundial shows time by the position of the Sun's shadow.

questions.q: How can you find the speed of a rolling ball using simple instruments?
questions.answer: Measure the distance the ball rolls with a measuring tape and the time it takes with a stopwatch. Then divide the distance by the time to find the speed.
keyPoints: Measure distance with a tape and time with a stopwatch
questions.explanation: Speed needs both distance and time.

questions.q: On a distance-time graph, the line for an object is horizontal (parallel to the time axis). What does it show?
options: It is moving with uniform speed
It is moving faster and faster
questions.explanation: The distance does not change with time, so the object is at rest.

questions.q: Which is faster: a cyclist at 10 m/s or a scooter at 30 km/h?
questions.explanation: 10 m/s is 36 km/h, which is greater than 30 km/h.

questions.q: A car travels 30 km in 30 minutes. Find its speed in km/h.
questions.answer: 30 minutes is 0.5 hour. Speed = 30 km / 0.5 h = 60 km/h.
questions.explanation: Units must be consistent before dividing.

questions.q: Which of these is an insulator of electricity?
questions.explanation: Rubber does not let current flow through it.

questions.q: A group of two or more cells joined together is called a:
questions.explanation: A battery is made of two or more cells.

questions.q: Which device works on the magnetic effect of electric current?
questions.explanation: An electric bell has an electromagnet that pulls the hammer.

questions.q: In homes, what do MCBs (miniature circuit breakers) do?
options: They switch off the circuit automatically when the current is too high
questions.explanation: An MCB trips and cuts the current in case of overload, like a fuse but reusable.

questions.q: Name two electrical appliances that work on the heating effect of electric current.
questions.answer: An electric iron and an electric heater. A geyser or a toaster are also examples.
keyPoints: Two correct appliances such as iron, heater, toaster, geyser
questions.explanation: These appliances have a heating element that gets hot with current.

questions.q: A fuse in a house circuit has blown. What is the right thing to do?
options: Replace it with a copper wire
Replace it with a fuse of the correct rating after finding the fault
Join the broken ends with a thick wire
Ignore it and keep using the appliance
questions.explanation: A proper fuse of the right rating protects the wiring, and the fault should be checked.

questions.q: How would you show that a wire carrying a current produces a magnetic effect?
questions.answer: Place a magnetic compass near a straight wire and pass a current through it by closing the switch. The compass needle deflects, showing a magnetic effect of the current. When the switch is opened, the needle returns to its original position.
questions.explanation: This is the experiment that Oersted performed.

questions.q: Which of these is a luminous object?
questions.explanation: The Sun gives out its own light, so it is luminous; the Moon only reflects sunlight.

questions.q: Frosted glass lets some light pass but we cannot see clearly through it. It is:
questions.explanation: A translucent material allows only part of the light to pass.

questions.q: An image that can be obtained on a screen is called:
questions.explanation: A real image is formed where rays actually meet, so it can be caught on a screen.

questions.q: Which mirror always forms an upright, smaller image of an object?
questions.explanation: A convex mirror forms a diminished, erect, virtual image.

questions.q: State the two laws of reflection.
questions.answer: The angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection. The incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane.
keyPoints: Angle of incidence equals angle of reflection
Incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in one plane
questions.explanation: These laws apply to all reflecting surfaces.

questions.q: A candle is 10 cm in front of a plane mirror. If it is moved 2 cm closer to the mirror, what will be the distance between the candle and its image?
questions.explanation: The candle is now 8 cm from the mirror, so the image is 8 cm behind it and the distance between them is 16 cm.

questions.q: Why is a concave reflector used behind the bulb in a torch or a vehicle headlight?
questions.answer: A concave reflector with the bulb at its focus sends the light out as a parallel beam. This makes the beam strong and directed so that it travels a long way.
keyPoints: Reflected light forms a parallel beam
questions.explanation: A concave surface can turn light from a point source into a parallel beam.
